title: Imagining someone’s ordinary day
description: Kindness gets easier when you remember that everyone you meet is in the middle of a day you cannot see.

body.heading: The cashier’s Tuesday
paragraphs: The person scanning your shopping has already served two hundred people, two of whom were rude about things outside their control. The driver who annoyed you may be on hour nine. None of this excuses bad behaviour — theirs or yours — but it changes the temperature of your response.
Imagining an ordinary day is not imagination for its own sake. It is a brake on the story your irritation wants to tell.

body.heading: Everyone is mid-something
paragraphs: The curt email may be mid-illness. The friend who forgot may be mid-crisis. We judge others by their worst visible moment and ourselves by our full context; remembering their unseen context simply evens the scales.
You do not need the details. “They are in the middle of a day” is enough of a thought to slow a sharp reply by the few seconds it needs.

body.heading: Make it a reflex
paragraphs: Practise on strangers where the stakes are low: the slow walker, the loud caller, the person who took the last seat. Invent their ordinary day kindly. The habit, built on strangers, will be there when it is a friend whose day you need to imagine.
It will also be there for yourself. People who imagine others’ days tend to forgive their own more quickly, too.

takeaway: Before you judge a moment, remember the whole unseen day around it.
